title: Apply group dynamic principles in order to guide a group towards independence and sustainability

lessons.title: Why groups matter and how they develop
lessons.html:
Groups in agricultural development

Much extension work in South Africa happens through groups: farmer associations, co-operatives, dip tank committees, irrigation scheme committees, savings groups, women's vegetable gardens and youth enterprises. Groups allow farmers to buy inputs in bulk, share equipment, access markets and finance, learn together and speak with one voice. However, many groups formed mainly to receive grants collapse once support ends. The extension practitioner's goal is to guide groups towards independence: functioning, self-managing and sustainable without ongoing outside support.

Stages of group development

A well-known model describes five stages:

StageWhat happensFacilitator's role
FormingMembers are polite, unsure of purpose and rolesClarify purpose, build relationships, agree ground rules
StormingConflict over leadership, roles, money or directionHelp manage conflict openly and fairly
NormingAgreement on rules, roles and ways of workingSupport the group to formalise agreements, such as a constitution
PerformingThe group works effectively towards its goalsStep back, offer support when asked
AdjourningA project ends or the group changes formHelp review achievements and plan the next phase

Groups do not always move neatly through these stages. A new member, a leadership election or a financial problem can push a performing group back into storming. Recognising the stage helps you choose the right intervention.

Why people join and stay

Members join groups to meet needs: economic benefit, access to resources, learning, social belonging and status. They stay when the group continues to deliver these benefits fairly. If only a few members benefit, or if benefits are delayed for years, commitment declines. Understanding members' motivations is the foundation for building a sustainable group.

lessons.title: Group dynamics: roles, leadership, communication and conflict
lessons.html:
The forces inside a group

Group dynamics are the patterns of interaction, influence and relationships among members. Paying attention to them helps the facilitator understand why a group is succeeding or struggling.

Roles in groups

Members play task roles, such as initiating ideas, giving information and summarising, and maintenance roles, such as encouraging others, harmonising and keeping communication open. Some behaviour blocks progress, such as dominating, constantly criticising or withdrawing. Help the group notice these patterns and share positive roles widely.

Leadership

Sustainable groups have leadership that is elected, accountable and capable. Watch for risks: one powerful founder controlling all decisions, leaders chosen for status rather than ability, or the same people holding office for many years without elections. Encourage regular democratic elections, clear job descriptions for office bearers, and leadership development for younger members and women.

Communication and decision-making

Healthy groups share information openly, especially about money. Encourage regular meetings with agendas and minutes, financial reports read to all members, and decision-making methods agreed in the constitution, such as consensus for major decisions or a majority vote with a quorum.

Managing conflict

Conflict is normal and can be productive if handled well. Common sources in farmer groups include unequal contributions of labour, disputes over sharing income, suspicion of mismanagement and family or political divisions. As facilitator:

  • Address conflict early rather than letting it grow.
  • Create a safe space where each side can speak and be heard.
  • Focus on interests and facts, such as financial records, rather than accusations.
  • Help the group develop its own solutions and agree on them in writing.
  • Refer serious matters, such as theft of funds, to the appropriate authorities.

Group cohesion

Cohesion is the strength of members' commitment to the group. It grows from shared goals, early successes, fair treatment and trust. Celebrate achievements such as the first delivery to a buyer, as these strengthen identity and motivation.

lessons.title: Guiding the group towards independence and sustainability
lessons.html:
What an independent group looks like

An independent and sustainable group manages its own affairs, makes and implements decisions, generates or mobilises its own resources, resolves its own conflicts and continues to meet members' needs without depending on the extension officer or a single funder.

Building blocks of sustainability

  • Clear purpose and business plan: the group knows why it exists and how it will create value, for example a co-operative selling weaners collectively at auctions.
  • Sound governance: a constitution, legal registration where needed, elected committee, regular meetings and annual general meetings.
  • Financial management: a bank account requiring more than one signatory, cash book, receipts, regular financial reports and member contributions or savings.
  • Skills: leadership, record keeping, production and marketing skills spread across many members, not held by one person.
  • Networks: direct relationships with buyers, suppliers, financiers and government departments.

A gradual exit strategy

Plan your withdrawal from the start. Move from doing things for the group, to doing things with the group, to the group doing things itself while you observe, to the group acting independently and calling you only when needed. For example, in the first season you might organise the input order; in the second season the committee does it with your guidance; in the third season the committee handles it alone.

Avoid creating dependency. Do not chair meetings, hold the group's money, or negotiate deals on its behalf. Encourage the group to contribute its own resources, even small amounts, as this builds ownership.

Assessing progress

Use a simple group maturity assessment with the members once or twice a year. Rate areas such as governance, finances, participation, skills and market linkages. Discuss the results together and agree on development actions.

Key points

  • Groups develop through forming, storming, norming, performing and adjourning.
  • Members stay committed when the group delivers benefits fairly.
  • Watch roles, leadership, communication and conflict; address conflict early and fairly.
  • Sustainability needs purpose, governance, financial controls, shared skills and networks.
  • Plan a gradual exit from the start and avoid creating dependency.
